canonical_topic: LNG Value Chain: Liquefaction, Transportation, Regasification
definition: The physical LNG supply chain has three stages: cooling gas into liquid near production, shipping it in specialized tankers, and warming it back into gas near the consuming market before pipeline delivery.
core_idea: Each stage has its own infrastructure and losses: liquefaction plants near wellheads cool gas to -260°F for loading onto tankers; tankers must be specially insulated because some liquid methane still boils back into gas in transit, causing fuel loss; regasification plants at the destination store the LNG cold until it's warmed and injected into local pipelines.
key_points: Liquefaction plants sit near production areas and are fed by short-range pipelines from wells.
Cooling gas to -260°F for liquefaction is energy-intensive, and the resulting emissions count toward LNG's overall greenhouse gas footprint.
Tankers lose a small percentage of cargo to boil-off (liquid methane reverting to gas) during transport; faster voyages and cryogenic reliquefaction systems reduce this loss.
Regasification plants store LNG cold until warming it for pipeline delivery to end customers.
relationships: Liquefaction energy cost affects LNG's climate footprint
trading_implications: Boil-off losses and liquefaction/regasification energy costs are real frictions that reduce the effective volume and raise the effective cost of delivered LNG compared to the original wellhead gas.
caveats: LNG is not a lossless transport method — some cargo is lost to boil-off in transit, and considerable energy (with associated emissions) is spent liquefying and later reheating the gas.
